title: The copyright claims creators fear most: YouTube resolves them in one click with AI music

content_html:
For video creators, background music is often a minefield: a melody used casually can trigger a Content ID claim, and at best revenue is siphoned off, while at worst the video is taken down. On November 4, YouTube brought its "Replace song" tool, which eases this hassle, to creators worldwide—it had previously been tested in the U.S.

The process is straightforward: when creators receive an audio copyright claim, the tool instantly generates four unique royalty-free instrumental background tracks to replace the copyrighted audio; once the replacement is complete, the corresponding Content ID claim is automatically removed. In "Replace song" in YouTube Studio, click the "Create" button under the "Suggestions" tab to get four instrumental tracks of about three minutes each, and you can preview them on a loop on the timeline and drag to adjust the volume. Each is generated instantly by AI, independent of the others, and unlike any existing music library, avoiding secondary infringement at the source.

Preserve the mood, avoid the minefield—but for now it only handles "accompaniment"

YouTube's positioning for this feature is clear: without disrupting the video's original mood, it helps creators quickly swap in compliant background audio and minimizes how much copyright claims interrupt the creative rhythm. Behind this is the platform's idea of using generative AI to backstop compliance for creators—rather than deleting a video after the fact, it's better to swap the music in advance. But the boundaries are also clearly drawn: at present it only generates instrumentals, does not support vocals, and cannot produce full songs. In other words, AI can handle compliance for "accompaniment," but it still can't do the job of "songwriting."
